title: KV-locality-driven SLO-fair scheduler with eviction lanes
creator: Aditi Rao
body:
Summary:
We need a scheduler for continuous batching that enforces tenant SLOs while improving GPU utilization by leveraging KV cache locality. Current preemption logic is aggressive and blind to KV residency, causing repeated cold-starts and long tail latency for tenants with hot KV working sets. This ticket proposes a 'KV-locality-driven SLO-fair scheduler' that uses eviction lanes (soft/hard), per-tenant KV residency scoring, and a low-overhead admission controller to balance latency SLOs and GPU memory pressure.

Problem statement:
- Continuous batching increases throughput but requires preemption to meet latency SLOs.
- Preemption today ignores whether a request will hit the KV cache; evicting tenants holding hot KV rows increases subsequent latency and token cost.
- High churn in tenant KV residency leads to oscillations (evict -> cold miss -> refill -> evict).
- We need a fairness model that protects small/latency-sensitive tenants without unduly hurting throughput for bulk/throughput-heavy tenants.

Goals:
1) Reduce p99 tail regressions caused by KV-eviction churn under mixed workloads.
2) Maintain or improve GPU utilization and throughput (tokens/sec) in steady state.
3) Provide tenant-level fairness guarantees (weighted by SLA tier).
4) Keep runtime changes minimal and rollout via feature flag.

Design proposal (high level):
- KV residency score: runtime maintains a lightweight score per tenant representing recent KV hit rate and working set "hotness". Score is an exponentially-smoothed metric (0..1).
- Eviction lanes: introduce two eviction lanes: Soft lane (preferred, reclaimable, preserves hot KV if possible) and Hard lane (must free memory). Scheduler prioritizes preemption candidates from Hard lane only when soft reclamation cannot satisfy SLOs.
- Admission controller: when a batch is formed, the scheduler computes an SLO risk estimate based on tenant p99 budget, current queue length, and KV residency. If risk > threshold, it will: a) admit by allocating a temporary token budget and preferring requests with high KV-locality; or b) preempt lower-priority Hard-lane tenants.
- Fairness mechanism: maintain moving average latency per-tenant and enforce a max-fraction of preemptions per tenant over a sliding window. Use weighted deficit counters to bias admission towards under-served tenants (by SLA weight).
- KV-aware eviction policy: when choosing pages/segments to evict, favor tenants with low residency score and high cold miss cost <= eviction_cost = (1 - residency_score) * estimated_refill_cost.

Implementation plan (components):
1) Scheduler: add KV score table and eviction lane assignment logic. Low CPU overhead, vectorized arithmetic.
2) KV manager: expose per-tenant stats (approx hit rate, bytes resident) via a compact API. Add soft/hard annotations to leases.
3) Metrics: new metrics: tenant_kv_residency, evictions_soft, evictions_hard, preemptions_by_tenant, admission_rejected, slo_risk_score.
4) Config: rollout behind feature flag runtime.slo_kv_scheduler, with knobs for thresholds and lane sizes.

Acceptance criteria:
- Under mixed small/large tenant bench, p99 latency for latency-tier tenants improves or stays within 5% of baseline while overall throughput remains within +/- 5%.
- KV churn (bytes evicted per minute) is reduced by >= 20% compared to current scheduler under our synthetic mix.
- No tenant sees more than X% (configurable) increase in observed preemptions compared to baseline; fairness index (Jain's) should improve for latency-tier tenants.
- End-to-end tests and canary deployment succeed without major incidents.

Testing and validation:
- Unit tests for KV score decay and eviction lane assignment.
- Integration tests with synthetic traffic generator covering: many small latency tenants + one large throughput tenant; long-running hot-working-set tenant; bursty traffic.
- Loadbench: run on staging cluster (autoscaler off) with 120 minutes steady-state and 30-minute bursts. Compare p50,p95,p99, throughput, and GPU memory pressure.
- Chaos test: induce transient KV store pressure and observe graceful degradation.

Rollout plan:
- Step 0: Feature flag behind runtime.slo_kv_scheduler = off by default.
- Step 1: Canary on 1 rack of dedicated capacity with low-impact tenants (2 days). Monitor slo_risk_score, preemption rate, evictions, and p99.
- Step 2: Expand to 20% of capacity for 48 hours.
- Step 3: Full rollout if metrics stable.
- Rollback: revert feature flag, which falls back to existing preemption logic. Pre-flight check: automated alert if p99 for any production latency-tier tenant regresses > 15% during canary.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Threshold tuning: how conservative should admission be? Conservative tuning reduces throughput gains. We will expose thresholds and run grid search on staging.
- Metric staleness: residency score must be low-cost; we avoid tight coupling with exact KV manager counters to keep overhead small.
- Cross-node KV affinity: currently we assume per-GPU residency; multi-GPU sharding patterns may need later work.

Progress updates:
- 2026-02-12: RFC draft posted in Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.com/confluence/display/INF/KV-Locality-SLO-Scheduler (internal).
- 2026-02-15: Prototype scheduler added to branch runtime/feature/kv-slo-scheduler. Basic eviction lanes implemented, unit tests green. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4217.
- 2026-02-22: Bench results (staging) show 8% throughput retention and 25% reduction in eviction bytes under a mixed 60/40 small/large tenant workload. See benchmark dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/bench/kv-slo-0222.
- 2026-02-28: Design review with SRE and PM. Action items: add per-tenant grace window to protect recently-warmed tenants, and surface slo_risk_score in Console.
- 2026-03-03: Added grace-window logic and updated metrics. Running extended loadbench (120m) to validate steady-state behavior.
- 2026-03-05: Initial canary pre-checks passing on internal lab cluster; preparing canary run on dedicated-qa.

Review feedback and decisions:
- Decision 2026-02-28: Use soft/hard eviction lanes instead of quota buckets to allow graceful reclaim. (approved by runtime leads)
- Decision 2026-03-01: Residency score should be bounded and exponentially smoothed with alpha=0.2 as default. (agreed in review)
- PM feedback: expose a conservative default profile for customers on Dedicated and a permissive one for Hosted trials.

Artifacts and links:
- RFC: https://redwood.atlassian.com/confluence/display/INF/KV-Locality-SLO-Scheduler
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4217
- Bench dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/bench/kv-slo-0222
- Monitoring dashboard draft: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/kv-slo-scheduler

Next steps / tasks (owner in parentheses):
- Finalize config knobs and defaults (Liam).
- Add E2E loadbench job in CI that reproduces mixed-tenant workload (Sana).
- Add Console widgets for slo_risk_score and per-tenant eviction counters (Marta).
- Canary run and post-mortem template (Aditi + SRE).

Acceptance tests (explicit):
- Loadbench script PASS with p99 improvement or <=5% regression for latency-tenants.
- Automated integration tests validate that eviction lanes respect soft vs hard annotations under synthetic pressure.
- PR reviewed and merged with feature-flag gating and telemetry enabled.

Notes for implementers:
- Keep per-tenant in-memory tables compact: use uint8 quantization for residency score in hot path.
- Avoid locks on scheduler fast path: use RCU-style updates or atomic swaps for per-tenant counters.
- Provide a diagnostic mode that logs candidate preemption decisions to help tuning during canary.

If blocked: The KV manager needs a small API extension to expose approximate per-tenant bytes resident. ENG-61257 is tracking the KV instrumentation work.

Estimated effort: 8 points (scheduler engine changes + kv-mgr API + metrics + canary + dashboards).

Contact: Aditi Rao (creator), Liam O'Connor (assignee).
